subject: maths
pattern: Relations and Functions usually carries 6-8 marks in the Karnataka 2nd PUC maths paper: one or two 1-mark MCQs (types of relations or functions), a 2-mark or 3-mark proof that a relation is an equivalence relation, and a 5-mark question on showing a function is bijective or invertible and finding its inverse. Examiners expect each of reflexive, symmetric and transitive to be verified separately, and for one-one and onto to be proved with the standard steps.

questions.q: Define an equivalence relation on a set $A$.
questions.answer: A relation $R$ on a set $A$ is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive ($(a,a)\in R$ for all $a\in A$), symmetric ($(a,b)\in R \Rightarrow (b,a)\in R$) and transitive ($(a,b),(b,c)\in R \Rightarrow (a,c)\in R$).
A function $f:X\to Y$ is one-one if distinct elements of $X$ have distinct images in $Y$, that is, $f(x_1)=f(x_2)\Rightarrow x_1=x_2$ for all $x_1,x_2\in X$.
A function $f:X\to Y$ is bijective if it is both one-one (injective) and onto (surjective). A function is invertible if and only if it is bijective.

questions.q: Show that the relation $R=\{(1,2),(2,1)\}$ in the set $A=\{1,2,3\}$ is symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive.
questions.answer: Reflexive: $(1,1)\notin R$, so $R$ is not reflexive. Symmetric: $(1,2)\in R$ and $(2,1)\in R$, so for every $(a,b)\in R$ we have $(b,a)\in R$; hence $R$ is symmetric. Transitive: $(1,2)\in R$ and $(2,1)\in R$ but $(1,1)\notin R$, so $R$ is not transitive.

questions.q: Show that $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ given by $f(x)=2x$ is one-one but not onto.
questions.answer: One-one: let $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$. Then $2x_1=2x_2$, so $x_1=x_2$. Hence $f$ is one-one. Not onto: for $1\in\mathbb{N}$ (codomain) we need $2x=1$, i.e. $x=\tfrac12\notin\mathbb{N}$. So no pre-image exists for $1$ and $f$ is not onto.

questions.q: Show that the modulus function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $f(x)=|x|$ is neither one-one nor onto.
questions.answer: Not one-one: $f(-1)=1=f(1)$ but $-1\neq 1$. Not onto: $f(x)=|x|\ge 0$ for all $x$, so a negative number such as $-1\in\mathbb{R}$ (codomain) has no pre-image. Hence $f$ is neither one-one nor onto.

questions.q: If $f(x)=2x+3$ and $g(x)=x^2$, find $f\circ g$ and $g\circ f$.
Show that the relation $R$ in the set $\mathbb{Z}$ of integers given by $R=\{(a,b): 2 \text{ divides } a-b\}$ is an equivalence relation.
questions.answer: Reflexive: for any $a\in\mathbb{Z}$, $a-a=0$ is divisible by 2, so $(a,a)\in R$. Symmetric: if $(a,b)\in R$ then $2\mid(a-b)$, hence $2\mid(b-a)$, so $(b,a)\in R$. Transitive: if $(a,b),(b,c)\in R$ then $2\mid(a-b)$ and $2\mid(b-c)$, so $2\mid(a-b)+(b-c)=a-c$, hence $(a,c)\in R$. Since $R$ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, it is an equivalence relation.

questions.q: Show that $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x)=x^3$ is one-one and onto.
questions.answer: One-one: let $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$, so $x_1^3=x_2^3$, which gives $x_1=x_2$ (cube root is unique over reals). Onto: let $y\in\mathbb{R}$ be arbitrary. Choose $x=y^{1/3}\in\mathbb{R}$; then $f(x)=(y^{1/3})^3=y$. So every element of the codomain has a pre-image. Hence $f$ is bijective.

questions.q: Show that $f(x)=4x+3$ from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ is invertible and find $f^{-1}$.
questions.answer: One-one: $4x_1+3=4x_2+3\Rightarrow x_1=x_2$. Onto: for $y\in\mathbb{R}$ take $x=\dfrac{y-3}{4}$; then $f(x)=y$. So $f$ is bijective and hence invertible. Define $g(y)=\dfrac{y-3}{4}$; then $g\circ f(x)=\dfrac{4x+3-3}{4}=x$ and $f\circ g(y)=y$. Therefore $f^{-1}(y)=\dfrac{y-3}{4}$.

questions.q: Consider $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x)=4x^2+12x+15$. Show that $f:\mathbb{N}\to S$, where $S$ is the range of $f$, is invertible. Find the inverse of $f$.
questions.answer: Write $f(x)=(2x+3)^2+6$. Range $S=\{y: y=4x^2+12x+15,\ x\in\mathbb{N}\}$. One-one: $f(x_1)=f(x_2)\Rightarrow(2x_1+3)^2=(2x_2+3)^2\Rightarrow 2x_1+3=2x_2+3$ (both positive) $\Rightarrow x_1=x_2$. Onto $S$: by definition of range every $y\in S$ equals $f(x)$ for some $x\in\mathbb{N}$. So $f$ is bijective onto $S$ and invertible. Let $y=(2x+3)^2+6$. Then $2x+3=\sqrt{y-6}$ so $x=\dfrac{\sqrt{y-6}-3}{2}$. Hence $f^{-1}(y)=\dfrac{\sqrt{y-6}-3}{2}$.

questions.q: Show that the relation $R$ in the set $A=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ given by $R=\{(a,b): |a-b| \text{ is even}\}$ is an equivalence relation. Show that all elements of $\{1,3,5\}$ are related to each other, all elements of $\{2,4\}$ are related to each other, but no element of $\{1,3,5\}$ is related to any element of $\{2,4\}$.
questions.answer: Reflexive: $|a-a|=0$ is even, so $(a,a)\in R$. Symmetric: $|a-b|=|b-a|$, so if $|a-b|$ is even then $|b-a|$ is even. Transitive: if $|a-b|$ and $|b-c|$ are even then $a-b$ and $b-c$ are even, so $a-c=(a-b)+(b-c)$ is even and $|a-c|$ is even. Hence $R$ is an equivalence relation. For $a,b\in\{1,3,5\}$ (all odd), $a-b$ is even, so they are related; similarly for $\{2,4\}$ (all even). For $a$ odd and $b$ even, $a-b$ is odd, so $(a,b)\notin R$. Thus the two subsets are the equivalence classes.

questions.q: Show that $f:\mathbb{R}-\{-\tfrac43\}\to\mathbb{R}-\{\tfrac43\}$ given by $f(x)=\dfrac{4x}{3x+4}$ is one-one and onto. Hence find $f^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
One-one: $f(x_1)=f(x_2)\Rightarrow 4x_1(3x_2+4)=4x_2(3x_1+4)\Rightarrow 16x_1=16x_2\Rightarrow x_1=x_2$. Onto: let $y
eq	frac43$. Put $y=\dfrac{4x}{3x+4}$; then $3xy+4y=4x$, so $x=\dfrac{4y}{4-3y}$, which is defined as $y
eq	frac43$. Also $x
eq-	frac43$, since $\dfrac{4y}{4-3y}=-\dfrac43$ would give $12y=-16+12y$, impossible. So every $y$ has a pre-image and $f$ is onto. Hence $f$ is bijective and $f^{-1}(y)=\dfrac{4y}{4-3y}$.
